questions_and_answers.question_text: What does the adverb jiù stress when used after a time expression?
What is often used at the end of a sentence with jiù?
Name the three meanings of kào.
What are the two main senses of guǎn?
Write the Chinese for "I got up at five this morning."

answers.answer_text: Jīntian zǎoshang wǒ wǔdiǎn zhōng jiù qǐlai le.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Write the Chinese for "This is our own affair; it's none of your business."

answers.answer_text: Zhèi shi wǒmen zìjǐde shì, nǐmen guǎnbuzháo.

questions_and_answers.question_text: What does the colloquial Guǎn tā (ne)! express?
Write the Chinese for "You should know how to take care of yourself."
Is jiù stressed in this use?

answers.answer_text: No — it is always unstressed or neutral tone.

articles.text:
9. A: Sānnián yǐqián wǒ jiù bú kào  I stopped depending on my parents for
      fùmǔ shēnghuó le.              a living three years ago.
   B: Nǐ néng zìjǐ guǎn zìjǐ, zhēn  It's really great that you can take
      bú cuò.                        care of yourself.

Notes on No. 9

jiù: The adverb jiù is often used AFTER expressions of time, and stresses that the time when the event happens is comparatively PROMPT, SOON, or EARLY. This use of jiù has the flavor of "AS SOON AS THAT" or "AS EARLY AS THAT," but it can also be conveyed in English simply by putting extra STRESS on the time expression: "He's coming TODAY!" (Tā jīntian jiù lái le!) When used this way, jiù is always unstressed.

New-situation le is often (but not always) used at the end of a sentence in connection with the adverb jiù.

Míngtian wǒ jiù yǒu gōngfu,      I'll have time to go tomorrow
kěyi qù le.                      (that soon).
Jīntian zǎoshang wǒ wǔdiǎn zhōng I got up at five this morning (that
jiù qǐlai le.                    early).

kào: This verb has several meanings: (1) to lean against, (2) to depend/rely on, and (3) to be near/next to.

Bié kào chēmén.                  Don't lean against the door of the car.
Wǒde Yīngwén bù hǎo, xiě         My English isn't good. When I write
wénzhāng wánquán kào zìdiǎn.     essays, I depend completely on a
                                 dictionary.
Mài'āmì shi yíge kào hǎide       Miami is a city on the sea.
chéngshì.

guǎn: "to tend/take care of/look after/manage/run/be in charge of"

Nǐmen liǎngge chūqu wánr, shéi   If you two go out, who'll look after
guǎn háizi?                      the kids?
Liú Xiānsheng shi guǎn kǎoshìde. Mr. Liú is in charge of testing.

Another meaning is "to care, to bother about, to concern oneself with."

Tā bù xǐhuan guǎn biérénde shì.  He doesn't like to mind others'
                                 business.
Wǒ bù guǎn, suíbiàn nǐ.          I don't care. Whatever you like.

Guǎnbuzháo means "can be no concern of..., to be none of one's business."

Zhèi shi wǒmen zìjǐde shì,       This is our own affair; it's none of
nǐmen guǎnbuzháo.                your business.

The colloquial Guǎn tā (ne)! expresses brusque dismissal: "Who cares about him!"

zìjǐ...zìjǐ: "oneself." Use the pronoun wǒ for "I, me, my," but use zìjǐ or wǒ zìjǐ for "myself." Sometimes zìjǐ is used TWICE in the same clause, as in sentence 9B.

Nǐ bù xiǎo le, yīnggāi zhīdao    You're not a child anymore; you should
zìjǐ zhàogu zìjǐ.                know how to take care of yourself.
